name: Cape Henlopen
blurb: The biggest park in the state and the one where the Delaware Bay meets the Atlantic. Great Dune, WWII observation towers, a fishing pier, and a campground with a bike loop down to the beaches. The point is a genuinely wild stretch of coast twenty minutes from Rehoboth.

dogs.summary: Leashed year-round outside the guarded swimming beaches. Non-guarded and surf-fishing sand is open in July.

warnings: Ticks. Campground reviews flag them repeatedly, especially the wooded loops and dune scrub.
outstanding: Get the park office number and seasonal hours.
Confirm the fee band and the guarded-beach dates.

photos.caption: Salt marsh under cloud, with a tidal creek winding off to the left. Reeds up close, low woods on the horizon.

name: Delaware Seashore
blurb: Six miles of barrier island between Dewey and Bethany, ocean on one side and Rehoboth and Indian River bays on the other. The Indian River Inlet cuts through the middle of it. This is where most of the drive-on surf fishing happens.

dogs.summary: The surf-fishing and non-guarded stretches take leashed dogs all year — this is the closest legal summer beach to Rehoboth after Dewey.

warnings: Discarded fishhooks and cut monofilament line on the drive-on beaches.
outstanding: Get the park office number.
Confirm where the drive-on access points are and what a surf-fishing permit costs in 2026.

name: Fenwick Island
blurb: A quiet three-mile strip between Bethany and the Maryland line, immediately north of the Fenwick Island town beach. Ocean on one side, Little Assawoman Bay on the other. Much less crowded than the parks above it.

dogs.summary: Leashed year-round outside the guarded beach — and it starts where the Fenwick town beach, which bans dogs all summer, ends.

outstanding: Get the park office number.

name: Holts Landing
blurb: Small and quiet on the south shore of Indian River Bay. Known for crabbing and clamming off the pier rather than for swimming. The bay here is shallow and warm.

dogs.summary: Leashed. No guarded swimming beach here, so the summer closure that applies elsewhere may not bite — confirm before relying on it.

name: Trap Pond
blurb: The northernmost natural stand of bald cypress in the United States, growing straight out of the water. Best seen from a canoe or kayak. Campground, cabins and a boardwalk trail through the swamp.

dogs.summary: Leashed on the trails. Millpond water — read the bloom guidance before letting a dog swim in August or September.

warnings: Millpond. Harmful algal blooms peak here in late summer.

blurb: A 66-acre millpond with a trail all the way round it, plus the state's only water park, a campground and cabins. The most family-oriented park in the system.

name: White Clay Creek
blurb: Thirty-odd miles of trail along a designated Wild and Scenic river, running up into Pennsylvania. The best hiking in the state, and the closest thing Delaware has to a proper woodland walk.

blurb: A big former du Pont dairy farm fifteen minutes from downtown Wilmington, open year round. A large trail system, including a paved walking path that runs through the woods along the creek. warnings: Several entrances, and they aren't equivalent. The ranger station, gift shop and pavilion bookings are all at the main one.

name: Bellevue

photos.alt: Canada geese on a pond in winter, bare trees, picnic tables and a pavilion along the far bank, and a small child crouched at the gravel edge watching them.
photos.caption: The pond in winter. The geese are here in numbers and they are not shy, which is most of the appeal if you are three.

photos.alt: A small turtle with yellow throat markings resting on wet gravel at the edge of shallow water, among fallen autumn leaves.
photos.caption: A turtle at the pond edge in autumn. Not a promise — but you do see them here.

photos.alt: Shallow water over pale sand at the edge of a pond, scattered with sweetgum burrs, with turtles hauled out on a rock in the distance.
photos.caption: The shallow end, and the reason the turtle photograph exists. Sweetgum burrs all along the waterline — worth something on your feet.

photos.alt: Bare trees reflected in completely still water, with the corner of a wooden dock at the top left.
photos.caption: Still enough on a calm morning to hold the whole treeline upside down.

photos.alt: A pond in summer seen over a timber railing, willows along the far bank, flat water holding the cloud.
photos.caption: The same water in midsummer, from the railing. Willows the whole way along the far side.

photos.alt: A grey horse in a dirt paddock in front of a long single-storey stable block, with steel gates and rails enclosing it.
photos.caption: The stable block and one of the paddocks. It's a working yard rather than an attraction, but you can stand at the rail.

photos.alt: A bay horse in a fly mask grazing in a fenced grass paddock in summer, with white post-and-rail fencing beyond.
photos.caption: Turnout on the grass in summer.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer
fieldNotes.body: No boat launch, no boat rentals and no pier — the pond here isn't that kind of water. There is a playground, and there are restrooms. All five had been sitting at "Not confirmed" for the same reason they were at Alapocas: DNREC's roster lists what a park HAS, so nothing in it distinguishes a facility that's absent from one nobody has checked. There is a park office too, on the right immediately after the entrance — what's still missing there is its phone number, which is a different gap from the building not existing, and the page said "Not confirmed" for both.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer
fieldNotes.body: Bellevue has working riding stables — a stable block, paddocks and a ring — and this dataset had no field for them at all. That is the same hole the playground fell through: the state parks type was built from what DNREC publishes, DNREC's park pages talk about paddling and camping and say nothing about horses, and so a facility that is one of the main reasons people come here had nowhere to be recorded. There is a stables field now, and Bellevue is the first record to use it.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer
fieldNotes.body: The pond is the other half of this park: Canada geese year-round and turtles on the rocks, shallow and sandy at one end with sweetgum burrs the whole way along the waterline. There is a pavilion and picnic tables on the far bank in the winter photograph, which is another thing this dataset can't currently say about a state park.

onSite.label: Park office

name: Alapocas Run
blurb: A wooded gorge on the Brandywine with a blue rock quarry face used for climbing, plus the Blue Ball Barn. Sits on the Northern Delaware Greenway.

dogs.summary: Leashed on the trails and greenway — but NOT in the playground area, where the sign bars pets outright and welcomes service animals.

warnings: No dogs at the playground. The sign at the entrance says "No pets allowed in playground area", and the park's own board lists pets among the things prohibited — along with bicycles, skateboards, rollerblades, glass and tobacco. Service animals are explicitly welcome.

photos.alt: A wide view of a large playground with brown ramps and railings leading up to elevated decks, a shade canopy over the centre, wood-chip surfacing, concrete paths and benches.
photos.caption: Ramps rather than steps to most of the upper decks, which is the whole point of the place. Concrete paths run right up to the equipment.

photos.alt: Playground swings in the foreground on dark poured-rubber surfacing, with a long ramped play structure, slides, shade sails and benches behind.
photos.caption: Poured rubber under the swings, not mulch. Benches face the equipment from both sides.

photos.caption: The sand area. The raised tables are high enough to pull a wheelchair under, and the sand itself is deep and clean.

photos.alt: Two children crouched in the playground's sand area, seen from behind and above, one filling a bucket and one turning out a red sandcastle mould, with plastic spades scattered around.
photos.caption: The sand is the part that holds them longest. Buckets and moulds get left out here and stay out.

photos.alt: Two signs on a post: a white one reading No Pets Allowed In Playground Area with a crossed-out dog, a small black plaque reading Service Animals Welcome, and a brown one headed Welcome, Prohibited In Park: tobacco, glass containers, pets, bicycles, skateboards, rollerblades.
photos.caption: The sign that decides whether the dog gets out of the car. Pets are barred, service animals are named as welcome, and the park office number is on it.

onSite.label: Can-Do Playground
onSite.note: A large accessible playground: ramps to the elevated decks rather than steps only, poured rubber under the swings, shade sails over the main structure, benches, and a sand area with raised sand tables you can pull a wheelchair under. Photographed August 2026.

onSite.label: Ninja Fit course
onSite.note: A blue steel obstacle course on its own deck, in the same field as the Can-Do Playground with a timber picnic pavilion between them. Signposted "Ninja Fit Playground". Older children than the main structure suits.

onSite.label: Restrooms at the playground
onSite.note: Between the Can-Do Playground and the Ninja Fit course, and well kept. This is separate from the Blue Ball Barn, which is a walk away — you do not have to make that walk with a small child.

onSite.label: The trails, by name
onSite.note: Alapocas Woods 0.7 miles, Upper Reach 0.2, Pawpaw Loop 0.3, Copperhead Curve 0.3, Forgotten Trail 0.3. The Northern Delaware Greenway and the Bancroft Trail run through as shared-use, which is why bicycles are normal on the greenway and barred at the playground.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer
fieldNotes.body: Restrooms, parking and the ranger station are all at the Blue Ball Barn. The paved trail is across the street from the barn.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer
fieldNotes.body: Alapocas Run has the Can-Do Playground and this dataset had no field for a playground at all — the state parks type was built from what DNREC lists, and DNREC doesn't list them. It has one now. The signage is the other find: pets are prohibited in the playground area outright, with service animals named as welcome. That sits alongside "leashed on the trails and greenway", because the same board bars bicycles, and the Northern Delaware Greenway through this park is a paved cycle route — so the board governs the Blue Ball Barn day-use area rather than every acre.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer
fieldNotes.body: The Ninja Fit obstacle course is in the same field as the Can-Do Playground, not a separate park — I had them down as two places until the maintainer said otherwise. Picnic pavilion between the two, athletic fields beyond, all off the same paved path.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer
fieldNotes.body: No boat launch, no boat rentals, no pier and no disc golf course. All four had been sitting at "Not confirmed" because DNREC's park finder only lists what a park HAS, so an absent facility and an unchecked one looked identical in this dataset. Alapocas Run is a wooded run and a greenway with no open water to launch anything into, which is exactly the kind of thing a visit settles and a roster never will.

photos.alt: A dark metal sign on a dry stone wall reading The Russell W. Peterson Urban Wildlife Refuge, with a cut-out heron and cattails at its left end.
photos.caption: The refuge sign at the entrance, heron cut into the end of it.

onSite.label: The Riverwalk
onSite.note: A boardwalk and an arched footbridge run out through the marsh from the Riverfront.

onSite.label: DuPont Environmental Education Center
onSite.note: A four-story center on the marsh, run by the Delaware Nature Society rather than by the park.

onSite.label: Russell W. Peterson Urban Wildlife Refuge
onSite.note: The marsh the boardwalk crosses. Signed at the entrance.

onSite.label: Brandywine Park
onSite.note: Has the marble fountain, lawns and the Brandywine Zoo.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer
fieldNotes.body: The Riverwalk boardwalk and the arched footbridge run out across the Peterson refuge marsh from the Riverfront, past the DuPont Environmental Education Center. Brandywine Park at the other end has the fountain and the zoo.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer
fieldNotes.body: The printed Brandywine Park map carries both an Off Leash Dog Area and a Playground in its facilities legend, which confirms from the operator what the record already said about the off-leash area and adds the playground.
